title: Defensive, error-resilient classes
idea: Defensive design means each class checks its inputs at the boundary, refuses bad state with clear typed errors, and recovers only from failures it understands.
points: Guard clauses reject bad input before any state changes.
Private fields stop callers from breaking a rule behind your back.
A typed error with a stable `code` tells callers exactly what went wrong.
Retry only transient failures, a bounded number of times, never bad input.

hero.title: Where a bad call gets stopped

steps.caption: The caller asks the `Wallet` to pay 200 cents.
The guard checks the type and sign first. 200 is a positive integer, so it passes.
The domain rule checks the balance. There is enough, so the change is allowed.
Only now does private state change. Nothing outside the class could have skipped the checks.
Next call: `pay('50')`. A string is not an integer, so the guard throws `BAD_AMOUNT` at once.
`pay(900)` passes the guard but fails the rule. `NO_FUNDS` travels back; the balance is untouched.
The caller reads `e.code` and decides: show a message, ask for another card, or log it.

code.title: Guards and typed errors
code.caption: Try `wallet.pay(-1)` or `wallet.pay(2.5)`. Each is refused before the balance changes.

walk.text: One error class with a stable `code` that callers can switch on.
`#cents` is private, so no caller can set a negative balance directly.
One guard, reused by every method that takes an amount.
Check everything first, then change state. A failed call leaves no half-done update.
The caller catches and reads `e.code`, not the free-text message.

code.title: Retry only what is transient
code.caption: A timeout may pass on the next try; bad input never will. Change line 17 to `withRetry(flaky, 2)`: the second timeout is rethrown and the run stops there.

walk.text: A marker class says which failures are worth another try.
The loop has no condition. Each pass calls `fn` once; line 6 decides when to stop.
Stop at the attempt limit, or at once for any non-transient error, by rethrowing.
The flaky call fails twice with a timeout, then succeeds on the third try.
A plain `Error` fails at once, with no wasted retries.

pitfalls: Validate before mutating state, or a thrown error leaves the object half updated.
Never swallow an error with an empty `catch`; rethrow or handle it on purpose.
Retry only transient failures of calls that are safe to repeat, and cap the attempts.

quiz.why: The state changes before the check runs. The throw stops the method but does not undo the subtraction.

takeaway: Check at the door, fail with a typed error, change state last.

starters: Should I throw errors or return result objects in JavaScript?
